subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage:
Sunday: Trisha climbed out of the pool with blue lips, shaking all over. Her papa, Eshaan, wrapped her in the big towel and rubbed her back until the shivers stopped.

Wednesday: Backstage before the school dance, Trisha's hands trembled on her skirt, but she was grinning. Papa held both her hands. "Excited-shaky or scared-shaky?" "Both!"

Saturday: At Chacha's wedding party, near midnight, her legs wobbled and her chin quivered. Papa scooped her onto his lap, and she was asleep in a minute. Later he told Mumma, "Same shivers, three reasons. If it ever kept on with no reason, we'd ask the doctor."

qa.q: What did Papa wrap Trisha in after the pool?
qa.a: The big towel.

qa.q: What was Trisha likely feeling when her hands trembled backstage?
qa.a: Both excited and a little scared, as she says herself; her grin shows the excitement, and the trembling hints at nerves.

qa.q: What helped Trisha each time she shook?
qa.a: Warmth and calm closeness: a towel for the cold, held hands for the nerves and a lap for the tiredness.

qa.q: What would change if the shaking kept going with no clear reason?
qa.a: Then, as Eshaan says, it would be time to ask the doctor rather than only warming or comforting her.

grounding: It shows a young child's trembling coming from cold, excitement and tiredness on different days, eased by warmth and closeness, with a doctor for shaking that keeps on.

passage:
I'm Ritu, from the flat across the landing. This evening Abhinav tapped his elbow on the gate, not hard, and let out a wail you could hear three floors down. "My arm is BROKEN!" Between howls he peeped to see who was watching.

His mother knelt, calm as anything. "Let me see. A small bump. Cold cloth or a hug?"

"Hug," he sniffed, and it was over.

Ten minutes later his dad handed him an ice lolly, and he squealed as if it were his birthday. I couldn't tell if it was a show or just big feelings.

qa.q: What did Abhinav shout after tapping his elbow on the gate?
qa.a: "My arm is BROKEN!"

qa.q: What might Abhinav's peeping between howls suggest?
qa.a: He may have wanted attention and was checking who was watching, or he may simply have felt overwhelmed by a feeling too big to control; Ritu can't tell which.

qa.q: Which choice helped Abhinav settle, and why?
qa.a: His mother stayed calm, checked the bump and offered a simple choice, showing him it was small without mocking his feelings.

qa.q: How does Ritu see Abhinav's big reactions?
qa.a: Ritu notices both the huge wail and the huge squeal and honestly can't decide whether they are a show or just big feelings.

grounding: It is a neighbour's account of a preschooler's theatrical wail and over-large delight, and a parent's calm response teaching proportion.

passage:
"Oof, it's raining cats and dogs out there," said Hafsa Miss, shaking her umbrella in the classroom doorway.

Vishal's head snapped up. He climbed onto the bench and pressed his nose to the window, scanning the puddles. "Where? I can't see any puppies."

A few children giggled. Hafsa Miss came and looked out with him. "You're right, there aren't any. It's a funny saying. It just means it is raining very, very hard."

Vishal frowned at the rain. "Then why didn't you say that?"

"Good point," she laughed.

qa.q: What was Vishal looking for in the puddles?
qa.a: Puppies; he said, "I can't see any puppies."

qa.q: What does Vishal's frown and "Then why didn't you say that?" suggest?
qa.a: He feels puzzled and a little annoyed that the words didn't mean what they said, and perhaps embarrassed by the giggles.

qa.q: How can adults make sure a young child like Vishal understands them?
qa.a: Use plain, direct words such as "it is raining very hard", and explain a saying straight away when one slips out.

qa.q: How might Hafsa Miss feel when Vishal asks why she didn't just say that?
qa.a: She finds it funny and fair, as her laugh shows, and it reminds her to speak plainly with little ones.

grounding: It shows a young child taking a saying literally and looking for animals in the rain, and a teacher switching to plain words.

passage:
Note for Preeti's parents, from Irfan, art room, Tuesday

I found Preeti drawing a purple sun on the wall behind the easel. When I said her name, she froze, then burst out laughing, a high, shaky laugh, and hid the crayon behind her back. It did not look like she found it funny. I knelt down and said softly, "You're not in trouble for laughing. Walls aren't for crayons, though. Let's fix it together." The laugh stopped. She scrubbed the wall with a wet cloth beside me, very seriously, and then drew another sun on paper.

qa.q: What was Preeti drawing on the wall?
qa.a: A purple sun.

qa.q: What was Preeti most likely feeling when she burst out in a high, shaky laugh?
qa.a: Most likely embarrassed and anxious at being caught; hiding the crayon backs that up. A little mischief is possible, but it did not look like real amusement.

qa.q: Which choice helped Preeti feel safe enough to stop laughing?
qa.a: Irfan knelt, spoke softly, said she wasn't in trouble for laughing and offered to fix the wall together.

qa.q: What would change if Irfan had snapped, "Stop laughing, it's not funny"?
qa.a: Preeti would likely feel more scared and ashamed, and the nervous laugh might turn into tears instead of stopping.

grounding: It is an adult's note on a preschooler laughing nervously when caught doing wrong, where a kind tone helps her feel safe.

subtype: Hiding a grimace to be polite [Regulating]
passage:
Saturday

Dear Diary,
Saurabh Chacha came from Nagpur and brought me a jumper he knitted himself. It is mustard yellow with a green frog on it, and it is SO scratchy. When I opened it, my face wanted to go "eww". I pressed my lips together and said, "Thank you, Chacha, the frog is so cute!" He looked so pleased he did a little clap. At dinner Chachi's karela sabzi was really bitter, and I did the same trick. Tonight I told Mummy both real faces. She laughed and said I can always show her the real face, even when I'm polite outside.

Sharmila

qa.q: What colour was the jumper Saurabh Chacha knitted?
qa.a: Mustard yellow with a green frog on it.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila press lips together and praise the frog?
qa.a: Sharmila disliked the scratchy jumper and felt disappointed, but didn't want to hurt Chacha, who had knitted it by hand.

qa.q: How did Mummy handle Sharmila's "real faces"?
qa.a: Mummy laughed and said the real face can always be shown at home, so being polite outside doesn't mean hiding feelings from trusted people.

qa.q: How does Saurabh Chacha experience the thank-you?
qa.a: He looks so pleased he claps, so he feels his handmade gift is loved; he never sees the scratchy-jumper face.

grounding: It is a child's diary about swallowing a grimace at an unwanted gift and bitter food to spare feelings, while still sharing the real reaction with a trusted adult.

subtype: Smirk and sneer as social judgement [Interpreting]
passage:
Monday: When Jahnavi read her poem about her grandmother's goats aloud, she caught Afreen smirking in the second row, one corner of her mouth pulled up. Jahnavi's cheeks burned. She's laughing at me. She didn't speak to Afreen all day.

Wednesday: The teacher called Afreen to solve a sum on the board. Jahnavi watched her walk up. There it was again, the same lopsided smirk, while Afreen's chalk hand shook and she got the sum wrong.

Friday: At the water tap, Jahnavi asked straight out, "Why did you smirk at my poem?"

Afreen went red. "Did I? I do that face when I'm nervous. I was next to read."

Jahnavi thought about the chalk and the shaking hand.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi's poem about?
qa.a: Her grandmother's goats.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi feel when she first saw Afreen's smirk on Monday?
qa.a: She felt hurt and embarrassed, sure she was being mocked, which is why her cheeks burned and she avoided Afreen all day.

qa.q: Which choice helped Jahnavi understand the smirk, and why?
qa.a: Watching Afreen in another moment and then asking directly; the shaking hand and Afreen's answer showed the look could mean nerves, not an insult.

qa.q: What is it like for Afreen to have a nervous face that looks like a smirk?
qa.a: Afreen may not even know the face shows, so she can be misread as rude and lose friends without meaning anything unkind.

grounding: It shows a school-age child reading a classmate's smirk as mockery, then watching more and asking, and finding it was nervousness.

passage:
My name is Ishita, and last summer we moved to a building in Kochi where I knew nobody. The first evening, the lady from upstairs, Mrs Elizabeth, came down with a plate of banana fritters. Mummy nudged me. "Say hello properly, smile nicely!"

I gave my small smile, lips shut, and looked at the fritters. Mummy sighed, but Mrs Elizabeth just said, "Take your time, I'm not going anywhere."

She came again on Sunday, and again after that. By the third plate I was telling her about my rabbit, and my smile had teeth in it.

qa.q: What did Mrs Elizabeth bring down the first evening?
qa.a: A plate of banana fritters.

qa.q: What was Ishita most likely feeling behind the small, closed-mouth smile that first evening?
qa.a: Shyness and politeness with a stranger in a new place rather than delight; looking at the fritters instead of her face suggests Ishita felt a bit nervous 🙂

qa.q: How could Mummy handle Ishita's shy smile differently?
qa.a: Instead of pushing for a bigger smile, give Ishita time, as Mrs Elizabeth did, and let the friendliness grow over several visits.

qa.q: How does Mrs Elizabeth read Ishita's small smile?
qa.a: She seems to see it as shyness, not rudeness, and calmly keeps visiting until Ishita is ready to open up.

grounding: It is a child's look back at giving a small closed-mouth smile to a new neighbour out of shyness, and being given time rather than pushed.

passage:
"Hemant! The pickle jar? All over the floor?"
"Sorry, Aditi Maasi."
"And you're smiling? You think this is funny?"
"No, I'm not…" The smile stayed stuck on his face.
"Wipe that grin off right now, or no cricket for a week!"
"I'm trying!" His voice cracked. His fingers were twisting the hem of his T-shirt.
Aditi Maasi stopped. "Hemant… is that a scared smile?"
He nodded hard, eyes wet. "It just comes when you're angry."
She let out a long breath. "Okay. I'm cross about the jar, not at you. I'll pick up the glass. You bring the dustpan."

qa.q: What had fallen all over the floor?
qa.a: The pickle jar.

qa.q: What was Hemant most likely feeling behind his smile?
qa.a: He was frightened and embarrassed, and perhaps hoping to calm Aditi Maasi down, not amused; his cracking voice, twisting fingers and wet eyes show it.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Aditi Maasi read the smile as cheek and threatened a punishment; noticing his twisting fingers and asking about the smile let her separate the jar from the child.

qa.q: How did Aditi Maasi see the smile before and after she noticed his fingers?
qa.a: At first she took it as cheek, as if Hemant found the mess funny; afterwards she saw a scared smile and softened.

grounding: It shows a child smiling nervously while being told off, and an adult who first reads it as cheek then recognises the fear behind it.

passage:
Monday: Sumit glared at the fraction problems, eyebrows crunched together, pencil tapping. Vikas, his desk partner, had just borrowed his eraser. He slid it back quietly and shifted to the far end of the bench.

Tuesday: "Ma'am, Sumit's angry with me. He keeps giving me that look." Mrs Pillai watched Sumit frown at a word problem. "Sumit, what are you thinking about?" "Whether it's three-fourths or four-thirds." She turned to Vikas. "That's his working-it-out face. Sumit, maybe tell Vikas that."

Thursday: Sumit's brow knotted over long division. Vikas leaned in. "Thinking face or angry face?"
"Thinking face. Help me?"

qa.q: What was Sumit trying to decide on Tuesday?
qa.a: Whether it's three-fourths or four-thirds.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when he slid the eraser back and moved to the far end of the bench?
qa.a: Vikas felt worried and a bit hurt, believing Sumit was angry about the borrowed eraser.

qa.q: What helped clear up the misunderstanding?
qa.a: Mrs Pillai asked Sumit what he was thinking and explained that the face meant working it out, so Vikas could ask instead of guessing.

qa.q: What would change if no one had asked Sumit about the frown?
qa.a: Vikas might keep avoiding the desk, and Sumit could lose a partner without ever knowing why.

grounding: It shows a child's furrowed brow over maths being misread by a classmate as anger, and an explanation that it means thinking preventing friction.

passage: "Lalremsiami, come and sit. When I, your grandmother Sabina, was about your age, at the school up the hill in Aizawl, our teacher had a famous eyebrow. One day I handed in my sums, smudged and half in pencil. He looked at the page, then at me, and up went one eyebrow. My stomach dropped. I was sure he was furious, and I nearly ran out of the room. But I made myself speak: our lamp had run out of kerosene, so I had finished by the window at dawn. The eyebrow came down. He nodded and said, 'Then next time, tell me first.' That eyebrow was a question, child, not a slap."

qa.q: Why were Sabina's sums smudged and half in pencil?
qa.a: The lamp had run out of kerosene, so Sabina had finished by the window at dawn.

qa.q: What did young Sabina feel when the teacher raised one eyebrow?
qa.a: Sabina felt frightened, with a dropping stomach, and was sure the teacher was furious, though the eyebrow could just as well have meant doubt or a simple question.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned things around?
qa.a: Sabina chose to explain instead of running out, treating the eyebrow as a question that deserved an answer.

qa.q: How did the teacher likely see the smudged page once Sabina explained?
qa.a: He understood the reason and stopped doubting; his nod and "tell me first" show he was satisfied, not angry.

grounding: It is a grandmother's memory of reading a teacher's raised eyebrow as anger and learning it was a question best answered with an explanation.
